Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The atomic bombings of Hiroshima on August sixth, 1945, and Nagasaki on August ninth, 1945, were catastrophic nuclear attacks by the United States on Japanese cities. They killed approximately two hundred ten thousand people by year's end through immediate blast, thermal radiation, and radiation sickness. The bombings hastened Japan's surrender and initiated the nuclear age, raising enduring questions about military necessity, civilian casualties, and the moral legitimacy of weapons of mass destruction.

The bombs, nicknamed Little Boy over Hiroshima and Fat Man over Nagasaki, were the only nuclear weapons ever used in warfare. They represented the climactic application of atomic physics to military ends. The blast destroyed the vast majority of buildings within a mile radius. The intense heat ignited fires that created firestorms. Radiation poisoning killed thousands in subsequent weeks and months. Estimates vary, but approximately seventy to eighty thousand people died instantly at Hiroshima, with total deaths from injuries and radiation by year's end reaching roughly one hundred forty thousand. Nagasaki's toll was approximately seventy-four thousand total deaths.

President Harry Truman authorized the bombings ostensibly to avoid a costly invasion of the Japanese home islands. However, Japan was already defeated and the Soviets were entering the Pacific War, so military necessity remains contested. The bombings accelerated Japan's surrender on August fifteenth, 1945, formally signed September second, ending World War II. But their strategic justification—whether a ground invasion would have cost more American lives—remains deeply debated.

Survivors, known as hibakusha, suffered lifelong health complications and social stigma. The bombings' aftermath demonstrated the long-term human cost of radioactive exposure and nuclear war. They galvanized the nuclear age, motivating global concern about atomic weapons, contributing to the arms race, and shaping Cold War strategy around mutually assured destruction.
